analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to trick banks into handing over someone else's financial records.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship on the first day of 1999, the bill was referred to the House Banking Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to trick a bank or other financial institution into handing over another person's account records — for example, by lying to an employee or using forged documents. Violators would face civil lawsuits, fines, and up to five years in prison, with state attorneys general also able to sue. It was introduced at the start of 1999 and sent to the House Banking Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers whose account information could be pulled by fraudsters impersonating them or their institutions. The bill would make it a federal crime to obtain customer financial information by false pretenses, create civil liability for anyone who does it, and let state attorneys general sue violators for up to $1,000 per violation. Banks and credit unions would also gain, since the same schemes defraud them.

how_it_helps.text: It would be a federal violation to obtain or solicit a financial institution's customer information by knowingly lying to the institution or its customers, or by providing forged, stolen, or fraudulent documents to get the records released.
Violators would face criminal penalties of up to five years in prison, rising to ten years in aggravated cases such as schemes involving more than $100,000 over twelve months.

Anyone who violated the rules would be civilly liable for actual damages or whatever they received through the scheme, plus court-allowed additional damages and attorneys' fees, enforceable by the affected customers and institutions.
State attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of residents for up to $1,000 per violation, with attorney fees awarded, and state laws giving greater privacy protection would be preserved.
The Federal Trade Commission and the federal banking regulators would enforce the rules, and the Comptroller General would report to Congress within 18 months on whether the remedies were adequate.

analysis.who_pays: People and firms that obtain bank customer records through deception — private investigators, information brokers, and others — would face federal civil liability, fines, and up to five years in prison (ten in aggravated cases). Financial institutions would bear the modest cost of complying with new regulator advisories on detecting these schemes.

drawbacks.text: The bill only bans obtaining records through fraud. It does nothing to stop financial institutions from voluntarily sharing or selling their customers' information to outside companies, so it leaves the largest commercial privacy concern untouched.

It carves out broad exemptions: law enforcement agencies are fully excluded, and financial institutions may obtain customer information in the course of 'testing security procedures' or investigating their own employees, loopholes a bad actor could exploit.

While state attorneys general can sue, the bill requires them to give federal regulators prior notice, lets those regulators intervene, and bars state suits against a defendant while a federal action over the same alleged violations is pending, limiting state-level enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, low-cost fix to a real problem — fraudsters and data brokers tricking banks into turning over customers' financial records — with meaningful penalties and genuine state and private enforcement teeth. But it is a narrow remedy: it addresses only deceptive extraction of records and says nothing about the broader practice of banks sharing or selling customer data with other companies. An honest supporter would acknowledge that it protects customers from outsiders while leaving the institutions themselves free to move the same information for commercial purposes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again before the Congress ended, so it died in committee.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 6, 1999, the opening day of the 106th Congress, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services.
The action history records no activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the remaining two years of the Congress.
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, meaning any version would have needed to be reintroduced from scratch.

Had it become law, it would have added a privacy-protection title to the Consumer Credit Protection Act, enforced by the FTC and federal banking regulators, with civil and criminal penalties for obtaining customer financial information under false pretenses.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms and individuals who obtained bank customer records by deception faced no new federal penalties, because the bill never moved. Consumers received no added protection against pretexting from this bill.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction: Republicans Marge Roukema, Rick Lazio, and Michael Castle, and Democrats John LaFalce, Maurice Hinchey, and Bruce Vento.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.role: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after its referral on January 6, 1999 — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split between three Republicans and three Democrats, and no opposition is recorded anywhere in the bill's history; it stalled without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Retail banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would make it a crime to fraudulently extract their customers' records, protecting both the institutions and the people who bank with them. Its limits cut the other way for consumers: it does nothing about banks voluntarily sharing or selling customer information, which is the other major privacy threat in this space.

Obtaining bank records through deception — a practice known in the industry as pretexting — would become a federal violation carrying civil damages, fines, and prison time, cutting off a business built on buying such records. These firms' gain came at customers' expense, so the bill's interest runs against theirs.
